newsitem.title: USA: Scientists find stellar 'baby boom' after Big Bang.
newsitem.headline: Scientists find stellar 'baby boom' after Big Bang.

text.p: A heavenly "baby boom" of stars occurred relatively soon after the theoretical Big Bang that gave birth to the universe, U.S. astronomers reported on Tuesday.

Using the orbiting Hubble Space Telescope to look back in distance and time to some of the dimmest early galaxies, researchers at the Space Telescope Science Institute found the star boom probably peaked around 3 billion years after the Big Bang, the cosmic explosion that gave rise to the universe.
Astronomer Piero Madao said the Hubble data showed star formation beginning to increase rapidly about 1 billion to 2 billion years after that first blast.

Using both Hubble and ground-based telescopes, Madao and his colleagues found about 15 galaxies that existed in the universe's early days -- around 11 billion or 12 billion years ago -- compared with the 70 star-filled galaxies present about a billion years after that.
The researchers were viewing the distant stars as they appeared billions of years ago since it would take that long for the light they emitted to reach the Hubble telescope.

The researchers tracked the rate of star formation in these galaxies by measuring the amount of ultraviolet light emitted from them and found these early stars were born at a rate a few times higher than they are currently.

These findings help to fill in the blank spaces in the history of the universe between the early cooling after the Big Bang, when matter was thought to be formed, and the emergence of stars and galaxies.

This research also supports the view that most of the stars that the universe will ever produce have already been born, meaning that most of the stars now alive are middle-aged or older, according to the Space Telescope Science Institute, a key centre for research on Hubble data.
Earth's Sun was born rather late in the game, about 5 billion years ago, the institute said in a statement.

But there is no upper limit set on how many stars the universe can contain, Madao said in a telephone interview from Baltimore. "At this point, we have no constraint on how high the peak is," he said.
The Big Bang is thought to have occurred sometime between 11 billion and 15 billion years ago.
